# Sipcode

> Free, open-source (MIT) command-line tool that reads your local Claude Code and OpenAI Codex logs and shows where your tokens and usage limits go. Zero network calls; nothing leaves your laptop. For Claude Code it also runs as a PreToolUse hook that caps verbose tool output and dedups same-session re-reads, and it exposes 16 MCP tools so Claude can read its own usage stats.

AI coding agents spend tokens and usage limits where you cannot see them: the conversation is re-sent with every request, files get read again, idle context rides along, limits change quietly, and an update can make things worse. Sipcode makes that visible from your own logs, with numbers checked against an independent counter that shares no code with it (`scripts/verify-counts.mjs` in the repo).

Sipcode is a context-hygiene proxy for [Claude Code](https://www.anthropic.com/claude-code), Anthropic's terminal coding agent. It installs as a PreToolUse hook and intercepts noisy tool output (git log, npm install, grep, ls, cat, find, tsc) before those bytes reach the model. Same-session re-reads of unchanged files are deduplicated. A Verified Warm-Fill step back-fills the dedup cache from the active Claude Code transcript on the first hook fire, so files Claude read before Sipcode was installed still get caught on their next read. The cache is only back-filled when transcript bytes match current disk after LF and BOM canonicalization, which gives zero false-dedup risk by construction.

On a locked, public, synthetic 20-task benchmark corpus (scripted transcript pairs, not recordings of live sessions), Sipcode's mechanisms remove 62.6% of tokens at the median (range 37.4% to 80.6%), totalling 3,567,170 tokens and $22.48 priced as Claude Opus 4.7. Anyone can reproduce these numbers with `sipcode benchmark`. Real-world savings depend on the workload. Anthropic's published research finds cleaner context gives a 29% quality lift and 40% fewer agent errors, which is the mechanism Sipcode targets.

Sipcode also reads OpenAI Codex CLI session logs for spend analytics. `stats`, `today`, `forecast`, `trend`, `impact`, `why`, `receipt` and `drift` accept `--agent codex`; with both tools installed they show one section per tool. Codex models are priced from OpenAI's API price table as of 2026-10-08, and a model with no known price is shown as unpriced, never as $0. The proxy, hooks and rules are not supported for Codex yet. `sipcode limits` reads the usage-limit readings Codex writes into its logs: percent used per limit window, when it runs out at the current pace, which sessions used it, and how many tokens 1% bought over time, with a cautious possible-limit-cut flag. `sipcode regress` checks the user's own Claude Code and Codex logs for regressions after an update and pins each one to the version. A Sipcode plugin for Codex lets users ask "how much did I spend", "how close am I to my limit", "why was that session expensive" and "did it get worse after an update" in plain words, in the ChatGPT desktop app or the Codex CLI; it runs the installed `sipcode` CLI locally. Setup: `npm i -g sipcode`, then `npx -y @openai/codex plugin marketplace add Anuj7411/sipcode` and `npx -y @openai/codex plugin add sipcode@sipcode` (no Codex CLI install needed), restart the ChatGPT desktop app, and ask in a new chat.

Numbers from the maintainer's own logs (one machine): 1% of the weekly Codex limit bought about 425K tokens (week of Mar 28), 357K (Apr 1) and 77K (week of Apr 13), about 5x fewer, which `sipcode limits` flags as a possible limit cut (always "possible": limits are account-wide, and Codex use on other devices or in the cloud looks the same). In 1.7.0 Sipcode found it had over-counted Claude Code tokens by 11.4% (resumed sessions copy earlier requests, and both copies were summed) and fixed it.

Sipcode launched on Product Hunt on Tuesday, June 23, 2026, and finished around #12 of 1,086 products that day (134 points, 28 comments).

Sipcode is solo-maintained, MIT licensed, has 2,409 passing tests, and makes zero network calls during normal use. A privacy test in the repo fails the build if any `node:http`, `node:https`, `node:net`, or `node:dns` import is added to `src/`. Your code and transcripts never leave your laptop.

## How Sipcode differs from neighboring tools

- claude-mem stores memory across Claude Code sessions. Sipcode is context hygiene within a single session. They are complementary.
- RTK (Reduce Toolkit) is a static methodology paper. Sipcode runs live as a PreToolUse hook with measured, reproducible numbers.
- codebase-memory-mcp is a RAG retrieval layer. Sipcode operates on what is already in the context window.
- Read-once tools rely on convention. Sipcode is automatic enforcement at the hook layer.

## Install

Node.js 20 or newer (Node.js 22.15 or newer to read the logs Codex compresses, `.jsonl.zst`).

```bash
npm i -g sipcode
sipcode stats
sipcode limits
sipcode why
```

For the Claude Code proxy hook, rules and manifest, run `sipcode init` (Claude Code only; Codex setup (rules, proxy) is not supported yet).

# Full README

## Install in 30 seconds

```bash
npm i -g sipcode
sipcode init
```

That is it. Your next Claude Code session will use Sipcode automatically. Verify a few minutes later:

```bash
sipcode drift
```

If the output reads `no drift, context health stable`, Sipcode is doing its job.

## What is Sipcode?

Sipcode is a free, open-source (MIT) command-line tool that reads your local Claude Code and OpenAI Codex logs and shows where your tokens and usage limits go. For Claude Code it also does three things:

1. It watches Claude Code's context window and warns you when it starts to bloat (context rot)
2. It catches duplicate file reads and other waste before they reach Claude, so you pay less for the same answers
3. It gives you receipts. Every saving is measurable in your terminal.

For Codex it reads only: spend, usage limits (`sipcode limits`) and regressions after an update (`sipcode regress`). Codex setup (rules, proxy) is not supported yet.

It is open source under the MIT license. It makes zero network calls during normal use. Your data never leaves your laptop.

## Why you probably want it

If you use Claude Code for real work, you have already felt this:

- Long sessions get expensive fast. A two-hour session on Claude Max can burn through a daily plan.
- Quality drops as the context window fills. Claude starts re-reading files, repeating itself, losing the thread of what was asked.
- You cannot tell what is bloat and what is signal.

Sipcode measures the bloat, then removes the parts Claude does not need. The savings are reproducible. Run `sipcode benchmark` on any machine and the same 62.6% median reduction shows up on the locked 20-task corpus. The corpus is synthetic: scripted transcript pairs, not recordings of live sessions.

## The two-minute tour

After installing, here are the five commands that show what Sipcode is doing.

### 1. `sipcode drift`

Tells you if the current Claude Code session is drifting from a normal usage pattern. Bloated context, repeated reads, stale signals are all flagged here.

```
Sipcode drift: no drift, context health stable vs the recent baseline.
```

### 2. `sipcode proxy --stats`

Shows what Sipcode caught in the current session, broken down by rewriter.

```
Sipcode proxy, rewrite stats
  total rewrites:    144
  est. tokens saved: ~288,685 (heuristic)
  signal kept:       67% (med), weighted across all rewrites
```

### 3. `sipcode benchmark`

Runs the locked 20-task corpus and produces a verifiable savings number. Anyone, anywhere can run this and get 62.6%.

```
62.6%  median savings on a locked 20-task corpus
       range 37.4% to 80.6%   3,567,170 tokens   $22.48
```

### 4. `sipcode today`

Daily spend summary. Tokens used, sessions, output ratio, comparison to a 30-day median.

```
spend so far    $1.20    across 4 sessions
tokens so far   943.8K   output ratio 3.7%
```

### 5. `sipcode forecast`

Month-end projection based on the last 14 days.

```
projected month-end   $17,674   (range $14,139 to $21,208)
```

## How to install (more detail)

Sipcode works on Mac, Linux, and Windows. Node.js 20 or newer is required, and Node.js 22.15 or newer to read the session logs Codex compresses (`.jsonl.zst`).

### Step 1. Install Node.js

- Mac: `brew install node`
- Linux (Ubuntu / Debian): `sudo apt install nodejs npm`
- Windows: Download from [nodejs.org](https://nodejs.org/)

Verify: `node --version` should show v20.0.0 or higher.

### Step 2. Install Sipcode globally

```bash
npm i -g sipcode
```

Verify: `sipcode --version` should show 1.7.2 or higher.

### Step 3. Run `sipcode init`

```bash
sipcode init
```

This command does four things:

1. Creates a `.sipcode/manifest.md` file in the current project so Claude knows what the project is about
2. Adds a small block to `CLAUDE.md` (or creates one) with rules that keep Claude's replies terse
3. Installs the Sipcode hook into Claude Code, which is the thing that actually saves tokens
4. Marks the date so `sipcode impact` can show before-and-after savings later

### Step 4. Open a new Claude Code session

Sipcode picks up automatically on the next tool call Claude makes.

### Step 5. After about an hour of work, check it

```bash
sipcode drift
sipcode proxy --stats
```

If drift says "no drift" and proxy --stats shows a few dozen rewrites with savings, everything is working.

## What you get

| Feature | What it does |
|---|---|
| Context-rot detection | Warns when a Claude Code session is starting to behave worse than the norm |
| Re-read deduplication | Catches duplicate file reads and skips them, saving tokens and time |
| Compression-integrity scoring | For every saving, tells you what percentage of the original signal was kept |
| Spend telemetry | Daily, monthly, projected. All from local Claude Code and Codex logs, no cloud upload |
| MCP server | 16 tools registered for Claude Desktop, so Claude itself can read usage stats |
| Reproducible benchmark | A locked 20-task corpus anyone can run and verify |

## Frequently asked questions

### Is it really free?

Yes. MIT license. No tracking. No telemetry. No paid tier. Every line of source code is on GitHub.

### Does it send my code anywhere?

No. Sipcode makes zero network calls during normal use. Everything runs locally. A privacy test fails the build if any network code is imported into the source. Its caches under `~/.sipcode/` hold token counts, models and timestamps, never message text, and are never uploaded.

### Does it work with Codex?

Yes, for reading. `stats`, `today`, `forecast`, `why`, `drift`, `trend`, `impact` and `receipt` read Codex logs next to Claude Code's; `--agent codex` or `--agent claude-code` picks one tool. `sipcode limits` shows Codex usage limits, `sipcode regress` checks whether an update made things worse, and the Codex plugin answers these questions in plain words. Codex setup (rules, proxy) is not supported yet.

### What does "possible limit cut" mean?

`sipcode limits` counts how many tokens 1% of a Codex limit bought in each finished period, on the same model. A period that bought at most half the median of at least two earlier periods is flagged as a possible limit cut. It always says "possible": limits are account-wide, and Codex use on other devices or in the cloud raises the percent without leaving tokens in your local logs, which looks the same.

### Do I need the Codex CLI for the plugin?

No. After `npm i -g sipcode`, run `npx -y @openai/codex plugin marketplace add Anuj7411/sipcode` and `npx -y @openai/codex plugin add sipcode@sipcode`. `npx` runs OpenAI's Codex CLI without installing it. Restart the ChatGPT desktop app and ask in a new chat.

### How is it different from other context tools?

See the [comparison page](https://anuj7411.github.io/sipcode/compare/). The short version: Sipcode is the only one with a published reproducible benchmark, zero false-dedup by architecture, and mid-session install support.

### What is context rot?

When Claude's context window fills up with stale, repeated, or off-topic information, the quality of its answers drops. Sipcode measures this with `sipcode drift` and removes most of the waste with the proxy hook.

### Does it work with Cursor or other AI tools?

The proxy, hooks and rules work with Claude Code. Sipcode also reads OpenAI Codex session logs for spend analytics (`stats`, `today`, `forecast`, `trend`, `impact`, `why`, `receipt`, `drift` with `--agent codex`). Writing rules to `AGENTS.md`, registering the MCP server in Codex, the proxy and hooks, `estimate` and `benchmark` are not supported for Codex yet. Inside Codex, the Sipcode plugin (`codex plugin marketplace add Anuj7411/sipcode`, then `codex plugin add sipcode@sipcode`; desktop-app-only users run both with `npx -y @openai/codex` and restart the app) answers spend, limit, why-expensive and regression questions by running the installed `sipcode` CLI (`npm i -g sipcode` once). For Cursor, `sipcode rules --agent cursor` writes the rules block to Cursor's rules file; Cursor's session logs are not read.

### How do I uninstall?

```bash
sipcode proxy --uninstall
npm uninstall -g sipcode
```

## Commands

| Command | What it does |
|---|---|
| `sipcode init` | Set up Sipcode in a project (manifest + CLAUDE.md + proxy hook) |
| `sipcode drift` | Check if the current session is drifting from the norm |
| `sipcode proxy --stats` | See what the proxy caught this session |
| `sipcode benchmark` | Run the locked 20-task corpus |
| `sipcode stats` | Tokens and spend over a window, one section per tool by default |
| `sipcode today` | Today's spend summary |
| `sipcode forecast` | Month-end spend projection |
| `sipcode limits` | Codex usage limits: when you run out at this pace, what used them, tokens per 1% over time |
| `sipcode regress` | Did Claude Code or Codex get worse after an update? Each version against your other versions |
| `sipcode trend` | Track one metric over time |
| `sipcode impact` | Before vs after Sipcode comparison |
| `sipcode why` | Per-session forensics |
| `sipcode score` | Audit a repo for AI-friendliness |
| `sipcode receipt` | Generate a shareable PNG receipt of a session |

## Requirements

- Node.js 20 or newer. Node.js 22.15 or newer to read the session logs Codex compresses (`.jsonl.zst`); on an older Node.js they are skipped, with a warning at the top of each report.
- Claude Code installed (for the proxy hook). Sipcode also works as standalone CLI tools (benchmark, score, etc.) without Claude Code installed.

## License

MIT.

# MCP server

Sipcode ships a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server with 16 tools so Claude Code can introspect its own context hygiene from the chat.

## Tools

The session tools take an optional `agent` input (`"claude-code"` or `"codex"`).

- `get_sipcode_info`: version, install location, hook status
- `get_project_manifest`: the `.sipcode/manifest.md` for the current project
- `get_proxy_status`: is the PreToolUse hook installed and active
- `get_proxy_stats`: rewriter breakdown, tokens saved, integrity score for the current session
- `get_drift_report`: bloat, rot, and re-read pressure for the live session
- `get_session_stats`: per-session token totals and rewriter activity
- `list_recent_sessions`: paginated list of recent Claude Code or Codex sessions
- `get_today_summary`: today's spend, sessions, output ratio
- `forecast_monthly_spend`: month-end projection with confidence range
- `get_codex_limits`: Codex usage limits: percent used, run-out time at the current pace, what used them, tokens per 1% over time
- `estimate_task_cost`: predicted cost of a task before running it
- `audit_latest_session`: forensic audit of the most recent session
- `get_agent_score`: AI-friendliness score for the current repo
- `verify_sipcode_impact`: before vs after Sipcode comparison
- `install_proxy`: install the PreToolUse hook from inside Claude Code
- `uninstall_proxy`: remove the PreToolUse hook from inside Claude Code

## Wiring

Add Sipcode to the MCP config of any MCP-aware client (`sipcode init` checks the tool count but does not register the server). Claude Desktop config example:

```json
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "sipcode": {
      "command": "npx",
      "args": ["-y", "-p", "sipcode", "sipcode-mcp"]
    }
  }
}
```

With Sipcode installed globally, `"command": "sipcode-mcp"` works on macOS and Linux; on Windows use `"command": "cmd", "args": ["/c", "sipcode-mcp"]` (see docs/MCP.md in the repo).

## Privacy

The MCP server reads only local files: Claude Code and Codex session logs, `.sipcode/` state, the current repo. It makes zero network calls.
